text: 8:10 a.m. The board secretary reminds you the meeting materials were supposed to go out yesterday. The deck is two-thirds done. What now?
right: Have the team finish by lunch

text: The board chair calls before the meeting: “No surprises, please. What are you planning to say today?” You do have exactly one surprise. Reveal it now?
The CFO whispers by the elevator: “There’s a typo on the revenue slide — an extra zero. It’s already gone upstairs.” The meeting is in an hour. Fix it?
An independent director sent 46 questions on the report before the meeting. He wants written answers, “ideally before coffee.” What do you do?
Your assistant reports: the projector in the boardroom is dead, and the directors are already on their way up. The backup room is taken by a sales stand-up.
Board meeting morning. Your only decent jacket is at the dry cleaner’s until noon. All that’s left is a reindeer sweater from your in-laws. Your call?
right: Buy a jacket on the way

text: In the morning you read the minutes from the last board meeting. They say you “promised to double the margin.” You said “we’ll try to improve it.” Dispute it?
The board chair wants to “warm up” before the meeting and invites everyone for a morning jog around the business park. In suits. Run?
right: Wait at the finish with coffee

text: At the board meeting one director is dozing, another is on his phone, a third is arguing with himself. You’re on slide thirty of forty. Cut it short?
The board asks why sales fell. “The market” was already the answer last meeting. The honest answer: “We got the pricing wrong.” What do you say?
An independent director takes the floor and spends half an hour on how things worked at his company in the nineties. The schedule is on fire. Interrupt?
The board wants to approve your new strategy “in five minutes, it’s a formality.” The document is ninety pages and you’ve never seen it. Vote?
Mid-meeting the board secretary whispers: no quorum. One director “stepped out for a minute” forty minutes ago. What now?
The board wants the head of sales at the meeting “to hear it firsthand.” He’s on vacation at his cabin with no signal. What do you do?
The board chair wants “one number that explains everything.” Your dashboard has a hundred and twenty metrics. Which one?
right: Ask for a minute to calculate

text: Board members are fighting over a slide with the logo: some like blue, some like green. The annual budget is still waiting its turn. Step in?
At the board meeting your CFO unexpectedly disagrees with you — out loud. The directors perk up and reach for their pens. How do you react?
The board asks you to “briefly comment” on an article about the company in a trade magazine. You haven’t read it, and the headline sounds alarming.
Half the board joined by video. One director’s picture froze with his mouth open, and he seems to be against. How do you count his vote?
The board wants a “what if everything goes wrong” scenario. Your team believes such scenarios attract bad luck. Who’s writing it?
An independent director asks why the report has no “sustainability” section. There isn’t one because nobody wrote it. Your answer?
The meeting is in its fifth hour. The directors are demanding lunch, but there are three items left, all about money. Break?
The lawyer whispers: the vote on the deal should have been by written ballot, not in person, or it can be challenged. Everyone already raised their hands.
The board proposes a KPI for you: “board satisfaction.” They’ll measure it themselves, by feel. Agree?
In front of everyone, the board chair calls your strategy “bold.” You’re not sure if that’s a compliment or a verdict. Ask?
A board member pitches: “Let’s do what the competitors do, only cheaper.” The others nod. Your head of operations goes pale.
You click to the next slide at the board meeting — and there’s a leftover team joke about “Plan B: move to a tropical island.” Silence. How do you save it?
The board demands that every decision over $1 million be pre-approved by them. That’s roughly all of your decisions. Your reply?
After your presentation an independent director asks for your personal number “to talk without formalities.” Usually that means weekend calls.
The board discovered your policies haven’t been updated since the company was founded. One still mentions a fax. Admit it?
right: Say the fax is a style choice

text: The corporate secretary shows you the draft board resolution. Your name appears eight times under “responsible person.” Protest?
The board suddenly wants to “see the team” and asks for every department head to join the meeting. In fifteen minutes. Call them in?
During the break the board chair asks if you’re thinking about leaving. He says it’s “just out of curiosity.” How do you answer?
The board approved your plan with one amendment: “Do the same thing, but six months faster.” The team looks at you hopefully. What now?
A director joined the board meeting by video from his car. His audio keeps cutting out, then blasting. He seems to be demanding cuts to your budget. Ask him to repeat?
Evening after the board meeting. The secretary sent minutes recording your “we need to think about it” as “management commits to delivering.” Fix it?
8:30 p.m. The board chair calls “for five minutes” to discuss the results. You’re at your child’s parent-teacher meeting. Answer?
In the evening an independent director emails that he has “reconsidered” his vote and wants to withdraw it. The resolution is already signed.
left: Call and talk him out of it

text: After the board meeting your team is waiting in the meeting room to hear if their projects were approved. One out of five was. Tell them now?
After the meeting, the board invites you to dinner at a restaurant. Informal, but “everyone will be there.” At home, a cold dinner and a sulking family await. Go?
Over dinner a relaxed board member mentions that candidates for your job were already discussed last year. Your next toast?
The CFO writes in the evening: “You didn’t back me at the board today. That hurt.” Even though he’s the one who didn’t back you. Reply?
Right before bed, an email arrives: “Board questions, URGENT.” Inside: one question and lots of exclamation marks. Answer before morning?
Your inner voice sums up the board meeting: “Not fired — so it’s a win.” You could celebrate with the team or go to bed. Your call?
The board secretary needs forty pages of resolutions signed by morning, each on a separate page. Your pen is already skipping. Sign?
The board chair writes in the evening: “I want to drop by your office unannounced. I mean, consider yourself warned.” It’s tomorrow. Prepare?
At home they ask how the board meeting went. You honestly try to explain, but after three minutes your kid wanders off to play. Continue with the cat?
right: Edit your notes for the minutes

text: Late at night an independent director liked a competitor’s post about “the right strategy.” You noticed. Ask him about it?
In the evening the lawyer suggests checking every board resolution from the past year for formal errors, “just in case.” About four hours of work. Do it?
In the evening your deputy asks what was said at the board meeting “uncensored.” Half the discussion was about his department. Tell him?
7:05 a.m. The company owner sends a nine-minute voice message, recorded, by the sound of it, on a treadmill. The point is somewhere in the middle. Listen now?
The owner decides to come in at eight “to see who arrives when.” It’s 7:40 and nobody’s here yet. Warn the team?
A minority shareholder calls at 8:15: he read online that the company is being sold. It isn’t. How do you calm him down?
The owner sends a morning photo of someone else’s office captioned “This is how it’s done.” Beanbags and a slide instead of stairs. Reply?
The owner’s assistant warns you: the boss is “in a mood to change everything” today. You’re just about to bring him the quarterly plan to sign. Go?
Over breakfast the owner shares an idea: open a branch in the city where he spent his vacation. His one argument: “Gorgeous waterfront.” Back it?
right: Gently talk him out of it

text: Annual shareholders’ meeting morning. Seventy shareholders and one dog showed up for a room with forty seats. Not enough chairs. What now?
An elderly shareholder arrives an hour early and wants to personally “talk about dividends” with you. You’re rehearsing your speech. Give him time?
The owner writes: “I’m bringing my son to the meeting today, let him see how business works.” The son is nineteen and has opinions. Ready?
The owner warns his wife will attend stand-up “just to listen.” Last time she “just listened” and shut down a project. How do you prepare?
The owner is stuck in traffic and runs the meeting on speakerphone from his car. His GPS interrupts every two minutes. Carry on?
A major shareholder sent a list of ten “awkward questions” he’ll ask at the meeting. Number seven is about your company car. Prepare answers?
The owner decrees that from Monday, every morning starts with group exercises to the company anthem. The company has no anthem. Who’s writing it?
The owner called at 7:30 and spent half an hour describing a book he read on “teal organizations.” Now he wants the company “teal” by Friday. What now?
A journalist who bought a single share just to ask a question showed up at the shareholders’ meeting. His question is ready, and it contains the word “scandal.” Let him in?
left: Let him in, it’s the law

text: The owner says he changed the password to the company bank account this morning and wrote the new one down “somewhere.” Payments are stuck. What now?
left: Drive to his house for it

text: The founding shareholder emails in the morning: he doesn’t understand why the company can’t “just go back to how things were in 2015.” Reply in detail?
The owner wants to be added to the all-staff chat “to be closer to the people.” The chat will instantly go silent forever. Add him?
At a meeting the owner proposes cutting everyone’s bonuses “to perk them up.” He just got back from his yacht. Object?
Vote at the shareholders’ meeting: one shareholder demands a manual recount. There are two hundred thousand votes, and your staff would be counting. Agree?
The owner wants to personally interview your future deputy. The candidate is excellent, but supports a rival football team. What do you do?
At the meeting a shareholder asks: “Why is the office coffee so expensive?” The other shareholders perk up: it’s the first question they understand.
The owner asks you to hire his nephew: “He’s very talented.” The nephew has already quit three other companies. Take him?
The shareholders demand bigger dividends. The CFO whispers that then there won’t be enough for December payroll. Your answer?
The owner took you to lunch and talked about his dog for an hour and a half. At dessert: “By the way, you’re fired. Kidding.” How do you react?
The owner says the font in the report looks “kind of sad” and wants every company document redone in something more “life-affirming.” Comply?
An investor-shareholder in Singapore joins a video call at 2 a.m. his time and is annoyed by everything. Especially you. How do you play it?
The owner wants to rename the company because the old name “doesn’t pop.” His son came up with the new one. It pops — just not in any known language.
At the shareholders’ meeting two major shareholders get into a fight, and each demands you back him. Your move?
9 p.m. The owner calls from his country house: “Been thinking — let’s fire everyone who doesn’t smile.” By morning he usually forgets his evening ideas. Write it down?
In the evening a shareholder messages you directly, bypassing the board: he wants to “unofficially” hear the profit forecast. That’s insider information. Reply?
The owner invited you to his wife’s birthday. The gift must be “not too expensive, but not cheap either.” Your pick?
The owner writes at 11:40 p.m.: “You asleep? I’m not.” That’s it. A minute later “typing…” appears and disappears. Reply?
After the shareholders’ meeting, a pile of written complaints awaits you. One is about the room being stuffy. Answer them all today?
The owner invites you to his sauna in the evening “to discuss strategy.” You discuss strategy in the meeting room. Go?
Your kid asks who’s more important: you or the company owner. In front of guests. How do you answer honestly?
In the evening the owner sends a link to a course, “Become a Billionaire in 30 Days,” with the note “Have a look, it’ll help you.” The course is paid. Watch it?
The founding shareholder calls late at night to reminisce about how he opened the first warehouse “back in the day.” You’re in hour two.
Your inner voice wonders whom you actually serve: the owner, the shareholders or common sense. Today it was hard to do all three. Reflect on it?
Late at night the owner demands a report on the “team’s moral climate” by morning. There’s no data, but you can feel the climate. What do you write?
The owner went on vacation and asked not to be disturbed about anything. Tonight a big order came in that needs his signature. Call him?
right: Sign it at your own risk

text: The owner’s assistant writes in the evening: “The boss saw a photo of you in a restaurant. He’s asking why you’re not at work.” In the photo you’re with a client. Explain?
In the shareholders’ chat tonight, people are saying the office is “too luxurious.” The office is twelve years old and the roof leaks. Join in?
left: Post a photo of the leak

text: The owner decided to personally inspect product quality and is standing in the workshop at 8 a.m. with a magnifying glass. The shift supervisor calls you in a panic. Go?
In the morning you learn the shareholder meeting pack went out with an old password, and half the shareholders couldn’t open it. What now?
The owner wants “all of last year’s contracts, on paper” brought to him this morning. There are four thousand, in an archive on the edge of town. Bring them?
A shareholder sends you an article, “Ten Signs of a Bad CEO,” with four items checked off. No comment. React?
At stand-up the owner announces that the company is now “like a family.” The staff exchange glances: last time, that was followed by canceled bonuses. How do you follow up?
7:30 a.m. An investor wants to move the pitch from lunch to 8:00 “because I have a flight after.” Your deck is on your laptop, and the laptop is at the office. Can you make it?
The investment banker sends the “final” investor deck in the morning. It’s final number nine, and your old photo is back in it.
The CFO reports: there’s enough cash for four months if you stop paying rent. Investors promise a decision “soon.” Your plan?
The investor scheduled a call for 8:00 and has spent fifteen minutes trying to turn on his camera. His dog, in frame, now knows your pitch by heart.
The banker calls in the morning: a fund is ready to invest but wants “your team on stage” today at lunch. Half the team is traveling. What do you do?
Morning email from an investor: “Why don’t the numbers in your deck match the ones on your website?” The website’s numbers are three years old. Your reply?
A fund analyst, age twenty-four, asks at 8:15 for a “quick” ten-year cash flow model. Send what you’ve got?
An investor invites you to a morning meeting at the gym: “Let’s talk on the treadmills.” The last time you ran was after a bus. Go?
In the morning you discover photos from the New Year’s party were accidentally uploaded to the virtual data room. Investors already have access.
The CFO wants to call the loss an “investment in the future” in the investor deck. Sounds nice, but the auditors are laughing.
The round’s lead investor writes at 7:50 a.m.: “We’re still in, but let’s discuss valuation.” That means they want it lower. Call?
In the morning staff ask if it’s true the company is “raising money,” and whether that means everyone gets a raise. What do you say?
left: Promise a review after the round

text: At the pitch an investor asks a question you can’t answer: “What if a big corporation enters the market tomorrow?” The other investors wait.
The investor wants a board seat and veto power over executive hires. In return — money you badly need. Accept?
The banker advises raising the growth forecast in the deck from 30% to 70%: “Everyone does it, investors divide by two anyway.” What do you do?
At the meeting an investor spends twenty minutes on his past successes and never once asks about your company. Ten minutes left. Cut in?
The fund sends a term sheet: all good, but the fine print says you can’t resign for three years. Sign?
The investor wants an office tour. A programmer is asleep in the meeting room after an all-night release, and the kitchen has a mountain of dirty mugs. Show it?
At an investor meeting your CTO unexpectedly says the product is “still a bit raw.” Everyone writes it down. How do you save it?
The investor offers money on condition that you move into his business center. Rent is twice as high, and it’s forty minutes from the subway. Your reaction?
The fund wants due diligence and asks for access to all correspondence for the past three years. Your lawyer is clutching his head. Give it?
Over lunch an investor asks about your personal “stop-loss”: when will you admit the idea isn’t working? Everyone goes quiet and looks at you.
For a fee, the banker offers to “introduce you to the right people.” The fee equals a month of payroll. Agree?
The investor wants to see an “unpolished” version of the financials “to feel the honesty.” The unpolished version is a spreadsheet with accountants’ comments like “what nonsense.”
At demo day you get three minutes on stage. The timer is huge and already running, though the host is still talking. What do you do?
9:30 p.m. An investor writes: “Ready to sign tomorrow if you send an updated model tonight.” The model was built by an analyst who’s already asleep.
The investor calls in the evening: he has “slightly revised” the amount — downward. The whole round depends on him. Your answer?
In the evening the fund says the decision is “in final partner approval.” That could take anywhere from a day to eternity. How do you wait?
The banker invites you to a private investor party tonight. Dress code: black tie. You’ve never owned a tuxedo. Go?
The round is closed! The team wants to celebrate tonight. The investors haven’t wired the money yet, and it could still fall through. Celebrate?
At home your partner asks why, three nights in a row, you’ve been saying “pre-money valuation” in your sleep. Explain?
An investor writes late at night: “Don’t sell the company to anyone but me.” Nobody’s selling the company, but the offer is intriguing.
The CFO calls at 10 p.m.: “If the investors don’t come through, we can’t make payroll next month.” How are you supposed to sleep after that?
In the evening the fund said no. The email reads: “We loved it, but not right now.” The team is waiting for news. Tell them?
The investor sent the signed contract at 11:58 p.m. with a champagne emoji. You’re not sure he signed the right version. Check now?
Your inner voice whispers: “Wouldn’t a bank loan have been easier?” You haven’t slept properly in two weeks because of investors. Answer it?
A new investor sends a “partner questionnaire” for the morning: favorite color, favorite book and “three words that describe you.” Take it seriously?
Morning. The CFO suggests borrowing from one of the investors, with the office furniture as collateral. The furniture is worth laughably little. Sign?
The fund wants a video about company culture. The team must look “genuinely happy” on camera. Take eight; the happiness is fading. Keep going?
At a meeting an investor suggests you put your personal money into the company “to show you believe.” Your savings would buy a modest car. Invest?
right: Say belief shows in the work

text: The banker wants “one slide on synergies” tonight. You don’t understand synergies, and neither does he. But the slide is due by morning.
The investor forwards you a startup meme and waits for a reaction. The meme seems to be about your company. Reply?
Late at night the investor proposes replacing your CFO with “his own guy.” Your CFO has worked with you for ten years. Your answer?
An accelerator invites you to give a morning talk to aspiring entrepreneurs: “Tell us about your failures.” There are many. Go?
left: Tell them about all of them

text: At the signing, the investor asks for a pen and takes your favorite — a gift from your first team. Now he’s writing in his notebook with it. Ask for it back?
9:00, strategy offsite out of town. The facilitator hands out sticky notes and asks you to draw the company “as an animal.” Your deputy is already drawing a sloth.
The strategy director brings in the “Vision 2035” document. It’s beautiful, but there’s not a single number in it. The board expects it by Friday. Send it?
Very expensive consultants present a strategy in the morning. It’s almost word for word your memo from a year ago. Tell them?
The morning starts with a debate about the new company mission. There are seventeen versions, and every one contains the word “future.” Vote?
The CMO bursts in at 8:30: “We must urgently enter a new segment — gamer retirees.” No research, but plenty of enthusiasm.
Day two of the offsite. Morning team-building: build a model of the company five years from now out of pasta. Yours collapsed first. Symbolic?
right: Rebuild it with a straight face

text: The strategy director proposes switching to OKRs. You switched to OKRs three years ago and abandoned them two years ago. Again?
The analyst brings a market study: in five years your core product may be useless to everyone. It’s forty pages. Read it?
In the morning it turns out nobody in the company has read the three-year strategy approved in January. Including the people who wrote it. What now?
At the offsite the facilitator asks each leader to name “the main threat.” Three of them name each other. Step in?
The sales director thinks the “focus on big clients” strategy will kill his plan. He came with a two-hundred-row spreadsheet.
The board wants a “digital transformation.” You ask what exactly to transform. Answer: “Well, everything.” Where do you start?
The product team proposes pivoting the company “toward subscriptions.” Your customers are used to buying once every ten years. Green light?
The strategy director draws a two-by-two matrix on the whiteboard. Your flagship product landed in the “dogs” quadrant. The owner loves that product. What now?
The consultants propose cutting the product line in half. On the cut list: the product you built your career on.
In an anonymous survey employees write that they “don’t understand the company strategy.” One honestly writes: “There isn’t one.” How do you react?
The CMO wants to reposition from “reliable” to “bold.” Your clients are pension funds. Try it?
The board wonders why the strategy changed four times this year. The honest answer: “Because the board kept changing it.” How do you phrase it?
At the offsite everyone agreed with every point. Suspiciously fast. You suspect they all just want lunch. Test it?
The head of IT says the new strategy needs a new platform. Launching it takes two years; the strategy covers eighteen months.
The new strategy director made a company map on a two-meter sheet. It’s hanging in the hallway, and now nobody can get to the coffee.
The consultants want three more months and twice the money to “complete the diagnostic.” The diagnostic has run for six months. Extend?
9 p.m. The strategy director sends a fresh idea: “What if we became a completely different company?” He reached this conclusion while you were driving home.
Evening at the offsite. Dinner and campfire mingling. The CFO has grabbed a guitar and is singing about the budget. Sing along?
After dinner the sales director admits all the numbers in his strategy were “pulled out of thin air.” He’s a bit relaxed. Remember that?
Your inner voice suggests writing the strategy yourself tonight — no consultants, no offsites. There’s a notebook by your bed. Start?
At dinner you accidentally call the family vacation a “strategic initiative” and suggest “decomposing the itinerary.” Everyone looks worried.
right: Sketch a plan on a napkin

text: Rereading the strategy in the evening, you notice it has the goal “become the market leader” and the goal “be a niche player.” Simultaneously. Fix it?
In the evening the CMO sends a video explaining the strategy with a cat. It’s cute. He wants to send it to all employees.
A board member writes that he read a book on blue oceans and now wants you to “find your ocean” before the next meeting. Look for it?
right: Reply “On it!” and get back to work

text: At the morning meeting it emerges that every leader understands the word “priority” differently. Sales has twelve of them. What now?
First thing in the morning the CPO proposes a “pivot.” It’s the third pivot this year. The team is dizzy from turning. What do you do?
At 8:40 you’re handed “Strategy 2027” to sign. You don’t remember approving it. Turns out it’s last year’s, with the date changed.
The strategy director wants “Strategy Mondays”: every Monday, leaders spend two hours thinking about the future. Approve?
Walking past the board with the new strategy, a procurement employee asks out loud: “Why do we even need this?” Everyone turns to you.
The facilitator proposes a “Company Funeral” exercise: everyone writes an obituary explaining why it died. Half the leaders write the same thing.
The sales director threatens in the evening to quit if the strategy doesn’t change. It’s his fourth threat this year. What now?
You dream the strategy was finally delivered and nobody noticed. In the morning you have a strategy meeting. How do you get in the zone?
The board sends a link to a competitor’s strategy: “Why do they have one and we don’t?” Theirs just has nicer design.
HR proposes tying strategy to bonuses. Now every bonus must be justified by a strategic objective. Accounting is in shock.
In the morning the CFO says the new strategy costs three times what you thought. He recalculated last night “just out of curiosity.”
The company newsletter wants to interview you about the company strategy. The reporter is an intern, and her first question is: “What is a strategy?” Answer?
The consultants propose a new org structure. In it, your strategy department reports to procurement. Sign off?
The strategy director emails in the evening with the subject “Bedtime thoughts.” Thirty ideas, zero execution. Reply?
The analyst reports that every forecast in the strategy is based on a faulty spreadsheet with two-year-old exchange rates. The board approved it yesterday.
The board demands an “artificial intelligence” section in the strategy. Never mind that you sell construction mortar. Write it?
After the offsite every leader posts “Thanks, so inspiring!” in the chat and goes back to their old tasks. Pretend you didn’t notice?
In the morning marketing sends a “strategy in pictures” built around a mountain-climbing photo. The summit is labeled “40% profitability.” Approve?
The CPO proposes dropping your most profitable product in order to “focus.” The CFO is already sketching losses on a napkin.
In the middle of the night your inner voice asks: “Is strategy even a real thing, or just a fancy word?” You lie in the dark, thinking.
8:00 a.m. The CFO brings the draft annual budget. The “Other expenses” line is bigger than payroll. What’s “other”?
Budget committee morning. Every leader brought a request 30% higher than last year. The money is the same as last year. Where do you start?
right: Hear each out for an hour

text: The CMO catches you at the coffee machine: “I need double the ad budget, or I’m not responsible for sales.” No numbers, plenty of drama.
In the morning you discover next year’s budget uses an exchange rate from two years ago. The whole spreadsheet is now fiction. Recalculate?
The CFO prepares “optimistic,” “realistic” and “pessimistic” budgets. The board wants to see one. Which do you show?
The budget spreadsheet won’t open this morning: forty tabs, two hundred formulas and one circular reference somewhere deep inside. It’s due tomorrow.
The CIO submits a budget request with the line “cloud migration — ∞.” He explains it’s “a placeholder,” but the board likes specifics.
At the morning budget committee, the HR director asks for money for an “employee happiness program.” The CFO looks at you as if happiness just got pricier.
Accounting reports this morning that last year’s unspent budget “expires” on Friday. Department heads are rushing to buy chairs.
The owner looks at the draft budget and asks: “Why isn’t it 20% lower?” No explanation, but lots of emphasis. Your answer?
The CFO wants a “contingency reserve” in the budget. The board considers reserves a sign of bad planning. Include it?
Every morning this week starts with a “budget stand-up.” It’s day ten, and you’ve started speaking in spreadsheets. Cancel it?
The sales director brings his annual plan: sales will fall, but his department’s budget should rise. He promises to explain the logic “in plain terms.”
At the budget committee two directors are after the same money. Each says without it “everything will collapse.” The meeting is in its third hour.
The board wants the budget “on one page.” Yours fits on a hundred and twenty. The font would have to be indecently small.
The CFO proposes cutting the training budget to zero — “nobody studies anyway.” Two employees just signed up for courses.
Mid-approval, news arrives: office rent is going up 40% in January. The landlord apologizes with an emoji. Recalculate?
At the budget committee the logistics director is crying. Real tears. His budget was cut by a third, and he runs four warehouses. What now?
The chief accountant reminds you that half of next year’s budget must be approved by Friday or procurement can’t start. The board meets in two weeks.
An analyst finds that last year you spent 103% of budget, yet 40% of line items were underused. Money leaked somewhere. Investigate?
The CMO wants budget for a “viral campaign.” His last viral campaign only infected his own department’s chat.
At the committee it turns out every director padded their budget with “a little buffer.” Together the buffers add up to a whole other department’s budget.
The CFO proposes zero-based budgeting: every line justified from scratch. Department heads are already filing vacation requests.
10 p.m. The final budget has gone to the board. Five minutes later you notice one line was counted twice. Recall it?
The CFO writes in the evening: “If we cut the holiday party, the budget balances.” The party is the one thing employees look forward to all year.
Rereading the budget in the evening, you notice your own “entertainment expenses” line is bigger than the training budget. Awkward?
The sales director calls at 9 p.m.: he “forgot” to include an incentive trip for his top salespeople. He promised it to them back in spring.
At home you’re asked to draw up next year’s family budget. Reflexively, you ask for a justification for every line and a “cost-cutting scenario.”
Five people opened the budget file at once this evening, and now there are five versions of the same tab. Which one’s right?
The board returns the budget in the evening: “Too conservative. Where’s the growth?” A month ago they told you to be conservative.
Your inner voice counts how many budgets you’ve approved in your career. Twelve. Not one hit the numbers exactly. What do you tell it?
At 11 p.m. someone in the budget chat writes: “Guys, did we include sales tax?” Dead silence follows. Check now?
The chief accountant warns in the evening: if the budget isn’t approved tomorrow, he’s going on vacation and nobody will process payments.
The CFO suggests celebrating the budget approval at a bar. He’s the only one still standing after a month of reconciliations.
left: Go, just the two of you

text: The morning after the budget is approved. The first department head is already asking to reallocate money within his line. The year hasn’t even started.
The CIO reports this morning: licenses for software accounting can’t work without have tripled in price. The budget is already approved.
A procurement employee suggests saving paper by printing reports in a small font. He prepared an eight-page justification in a large font.
The CFO and the sales director argue over whose revenue forecast is right. They differ by a factor of three. Which goes in the budget?
In the evening you accidentally send the budget to the all-staff chat instead of the board. Now everyone knows what your company car costs.
The HR director wants a 10% salary indexation in the budget. The CFO says 5% max. The board says zero.
A board member wants the budget to include sponsoring a golf tournament. He plays golf. The business has nothing to do with golf.
Late at night the CFO proposes a budget with “a little trick”: push some expenses into next year. Technically legal, but the auditors will raise eyebrows.
In the morning you learn last year’s entire events budget went on one party featuring a magician. This year starts from zero.
Defending the budget, the head of production says the machine he’s requesting money for “will run another ten years.” He said the same thing three years ago.
The CMO sends a “revised” request in the evening. It’s 50% higher and includes a line for a “life-size company mascot.”
One department submitted its budget request as a four-minute voice message. The numbers are mentioned in passing, mixed in with the weather.
right: Send it back as a spreadsheet

text: In the middle of your budget defense, the power goes out. Your deck is on a laptop at 3% battery. What now?
In the evening a department head whose budget you cut calls to ask if he can at least keep the coffee machine. It costs as much as a used car.
The owner sends his version of the budget, hand-drawn on a restaurant napkin. The numbers don’t add up, but the handwriting is confident.
At the committee the head of security asks for money to put cameras in the meeting rooms. The other directors are suddenly opposed — even those who were silent all day.
The HR director brings you numbers in the evening: if the hiring budget is cut, you’ll be without two key people. Offers have already gone out to them.
Morning. Analytics proposes a new budget template with dropdowns, color zones and macros. Everyone knows the old template by heart.
Late at night you realize the budget only balances if every client pays on time. That has never once happened.
Your assistant brings budget version five, labeled “final_really_final_v5.” Version six is expected by lunch.
Tomorrow’s calendar reads “Budget. Final. Discussion 2.0.” You don’t remember what happened in 1.0. Prepare?
8:20 a.m. The CFO drops a list of “savings ideas” on your desk. Item one: turn off the air conditioning. It’s July. Approve?
The board demands a 15% cost cut “without loss of quality.” How exactly is left to your creative discretion.
The office manager reports: as a cost-saving measure, the kitchen cookies have been replaced with dry crackers. Staff have begun a quiet resistance, bringing cookies from home.
A new rule since this morning: color printing only with director approval. There’s a line of eight people with charts outside your door.
The procurement director proposes switching paper suppliers. The new paper is 30% cheaper, but the printers cough on it. Switch?
A sign in the elevator: “To save costs, the elevator operates from 10:00.” You’re on the eighth floor, meeting at 9:00. Who came up with this?
right: Take the stairs as an example

text: The CFO proposes ending company-paid taxis after 10 p.m. The people working late are mostly the ones doing your urgent tasks.
New rule this morning: economy class only, with layovers. Your sales director is flying to negotiations via three cities.
To save money, office heating now comes on an hour later. Staff arrived in scarves; accounting came in blankets. Work is crawling.
In the morning the company driver tells you the car was sold to cut costs. You learn this standing outside your building in a suit.
The cost-optimization consultant suggests starting with the big one — your office. He proposes you move into the open space with the staff.
A company-wide email this morning: subscriptions to professional journals are canceled. You were the only one who read them.
The CFO thinks you could save money by canceling New Year’s gifts for clients. Key clients have been getting them for ten years.
Employees drop their own cost-saving idea in the anonymous box: cut management’s pay. Forty people signed it.
A move to a smaller office is on the table. It’s half the price, but has just one meeting room and one restroom per floor.
The CIO proposes saving on licenses: “Half the staff use the software once a month.” Everyone else will wait in line.
The board demands a 10% headcount reduction. You must propose a list. It will inevitably include people you personally hired.
The CMO learns his budget has been halved. He proposes making do with “guerrilla marketing” and has already bought a costume.
The board wants to save on outsourced cleaning. Staff are asked to clean up after themselves on a rota. The rota is already posted.
A department head brings a layoff list with only one name — his own. He says it’s “the most honest solution.” What now?
The CFO wants to cancel the corporate cloud storage subscription. The whole thing is five years of office party photos.
The board wants a cost-reduction report every two weeks. The report itself takes three analysts to produce.
The HR director proposes canceling the annual party and holding it online. Last year’s online party ended after twenty minutes.
right: Do a modest one in person

text: The cost-optimization consultant has found that the biggest item of unnecessary spending is cost-optimization consultants. He suggests extending his contract.
Evening. The layoff list is approved. Tomorrow you have to tell people in person. One of them invited you to his wedding today.
9 p.m. You’re the last to leave and every light in the building is on. Just yesterday the board talked about saving electricity. Turn them off?
In the evening the CFO sends a spreadsheet: cutting office coffee would save, over a year, the equivalent of one quarterly bonus. Your call.
In the staff chat someone writes: “Meanwhile the CEO got a new office.” Your office hasn’t changed in ten years. Respond?
In the evening a department head begs you to keep an intern. The intern brings homemade pies and knows every password.
In the evening you discover that, thanks to cost cutting, the office is out of toilet paper. Investors arrive in the morning. Go to the store?
A board member calls in the evening to ask why you haven’t cut “the department that does nothing.” That department is accounting. Explain?
At home you absentmindedly turn off the light in a room full of people and suggest “optimizing” dinner down to one course. The family tenses up.
Your inner voice asks what you yourself are willing to cut back on. No answer. You look at your collection of expensive pens.
An employee emails an idea: sell the old office furniture and buy cheaper new furniture. The furniture is antique; the founder bought it.
After a hard day of layoffs, your deputy asks for vacation. He says he’s “burned out like a match.” Let him go?
8:40 a.m. Cost cutting has reached the water coolers: they’re gone. Staff carry plastic bottles and pointedly set them on your desk.
First thing in the morning the CFO proposes paying suppliers a month late “so the money can work for us.” Suppliers threaten to halt deliveries.
To save costs, you’re asked to hold meetings standing instead of in a meeting room, “to keep them short.” The forty-minute meeting lasted forty minutes, standing.
The HR director proposes announcing layoffs on Friday evening “so people have time to digest it.” You know rumors are already flying.
To save money, the server room heating was turned off tonight. The servers will be fine by morning; the sysadmin who sleeps there — unclear.
The company switches from paid to free video calls. The first meeting with a key client cuts off after forty minutes: “Time’s up.”
Instead of layoffs, the board proposes a four-day week for everyone with a pay cut. Employees say they like the day off more than the money.
The CFO admits in the evening that the money saved on coffee went to a fine for a late report. The savings never happened.
A sign in the kitchen: “Starting Monday, sugar is rationed by coupon.” Someone from accounting posted it, but signed it with your name.
The sales director proposes saving on client meetings by holding them in the cafeteria instead of restaurants. A key client is already on his second fruit punch.
An employee sends results in the evening: stationery savings for the quarter came to $15. Counting it took 80 hours of his time.
A guard at the entrance checks that employees aren’t taking office pens home. A decision by the previous CFO that everyone forgot about.
The board proposes canceling corporate health insurance. Employees find out on social media before the official email.
Evening. You tally the quarter’s savings. A lot was saved, but three key employees left for competitors. The net result is unclear.
A laid-off employee sent a warm thank-you email for his years here. You’re reading it for the third time. Reply?
7:45 a.m. The CEO of your biggest client calls personally: a three-year contract is ready, but the price must drop 25% “today.”
The tender team reports: the bid for the year’s biggest tender is due by noon. Three signatures are missing, plus a stamp locked in a safe at someone’s country house.
At 8:30 the lawyer finds a clause in a major supply contract: a daily late penalty equal to your annual profit. Signing is at ten.
The sales director is overjoyed this morning: he’s “nearly closed” the deal of the year. Nearly means the client said “interesting.” The board has already been told.
A key client sends a revised contract in the morning. Changes are highlighted in yellow. Everything is yellow except the parties’ names.
left: Read it with Legal all day

text: Negotiations with a supplier start at 8 a.m. in his office. You’re served tea in glasses with metal holders, and nobody speaks. Is this a tactic?
The CFO warns you first thing: if the big contract falls through, the quarter will be a loss. No pressure, just so you know.
Your joint-venture partner writes that he wants to “revisit the shares.” The project is profitable for the first time in two years. Coincidence?
In the morning you learn a major supply contract was signed with wrong bank details. The money went to someone who just shares the client’s name.
In negotiations on a big deal, the client’s rep steps out “to make a call” every ten minutes. You suspect he’s consulting someone higher up.
left: Ask for the boss at the table

text: The client is ready to sign a dream contract, but wants a clause: your CEO — that is, you — personally oversees the project. Weekly, on Saturdays.
You won the tender! The price is so low the company will break even at best. But the board wanted a “high-profile contract.” Sign?
The client’s lawyer sent a “small edit”: you’re liable for any outage anywhere in the world. Even the weather.
Talks are deadlocked. The client proposes settling it over pool: if he wins, you give 10% off. You haven’t played since college.
The sales director promised the client delivery in a week. Production says a month minimum. The client is happily signing.
Your deal partner proposes “sealing the agreement” with a hunting trip. You don’t hunt — you feel sorry for mosquitoes. Go?
A major client proposes paying in installments over two years instead of upfront. The CFO is already sketching cash gaps on a napkin.
In talks with a major client, your CTO starts arguing with their CTO. The client is enjoying the show.
The client wants exclusivity: you can’t work with his competitors for five years. His competitors are the other half of your revenue.
A government client requires forty-three documents to enter a tender. One is a certificate confirming all the certificates are genuine.
The deal is almost closed, but the client wants a “symbolic gift”: another one percent off. The CFO says that’s his annual bonus.
11 p.m. Contract talks are in their fourteenth hour. The client ordered pizza and looks ready to stay till dawn. Your team is nodding off.
The client writes in the evening: “We’ll sign, but only if your CEO comes to our party.” The party is tomorrow. The theme: pirates.
left: Show up in a tricorn hat

text: Evening: the contract is signed. You send the client the signed copy and notice thousands and millions got mixed up. In your favor.
In the evening the tender team wants you to personally sign four hundred pages of a bid. Each one. An e-signature is “not compliant with procedure.”
Your deal partner calls at 10:30 p.m.: “We’ve changed our minds. But not completely.” He wants to meet at 7 a.m. to “change them back.”
In the evening the lawyer admits the contract signed today isn’t the agreed version. One word differs: “may” instead of “shall.”
In the evening the sales director wants to celebrate a big deal at a restaurant. The client hasn’t paid yet, and he wants to bill it to the company.
At home they ask why you’ve been smiling at your phone all evening. You just received a signed three-year contract. Dinner is getting cold.
Your inner voice tallies: this month you ran twenty negotiations and won one. But what a one! Keep up the same pace?
Morning. You get a notification that the contract with a key supplier expires at midnight tonight. Nobody started renewal talks.
The client sends a “quick question” with twenty items. Each one begins with “Could you just…”
Tender lost: your price was one cent higher than the winner’s. The tender team wants a “one-cent buffer” built into all future bids.
right: Chalk it up to bad luck

text: A major client sends the contract as photos from his phone. Several pages were shot at an angle, and one includes his cat.
In the evening the CEO of a company whose deal fell through calls you. He suggests “starting over,” but for half the amount.
The head of the contracts department demands that every contract go through twelve signatures. A client deal has been waiting since Monday.
The client is playing good cop, bad cop. The bad cop is his accountant, and he’s very convincing.
In the evening the client posted a thumbs-up emoji in the project chat and nothing else. The signing was scheduled for today. Is that a yes?
The head of logistics reports: a shipment under a major contract is stuck in customs. The client expects it by lunch today.
A key client offers a ten-year contract, but with annual price indexation of just 1%. Your inflation is higher.
Late in the evening the print shop calls: the gold-embossed commemorative copies of the contract were printed with the client’s name misspelled.
The sales director admits he promised the client five years of free maintenance. Out loud. Nothing in writing.
The client invited you to his office for the signing. The pen you’re offered doesn’t write. The client considers this a bad omen.
In the evening your deal partner suggests “celebrating” at his place. His wife already cooked dinner for twelve, and your family is waiting for you.
Negotiation morning. The client proposes holding the talks in French, though everyone at the table speaks English. It’s “more distinguished.” Agree?
Your inner voice reminds you that you never read Appendix 7 of the contract you signed today. Now you can’t sleep.
The tender winner backed out, and the contract is offered to you at your price. Except it’s due in a week, not a month like in your bid.
Morning. The lawyer reports your biggest contract can be terminated with a single letter if the client “loses interest.” The client was yawning at the last meeting.
The client offers to double the deal if you agree to his terms right now, without the board. Your authority only covers half.
An e-contract arrives for signature, due by midnight. The link leads to a page that won’t open in your browser.
7:20 a.m. The investment bank reports a big corporation wants to buy your company. It must stay secret, even from your own deputies. Can you manage?
First morning after the merger. The lobby has two reception desks, two logos and two security guards who won’t let in staff from the “other” company.
The board proposes buying a small competitor. Great team, but their office is in a basement and they owe the landlord.
Due diligence begins on the company you’re buying. Their CFO brought the documents in shoeboxes labeled in marker.
First joint meeting of the merged teams. One side arrives at 9:00, the other at 10:00. Each thinks their schedule is the right one.
A competitor proposes a merger “of equals.” His revenue is a third of yours, but he believes he’s three times smarter. Meet?
The morning after the merger announcement, staff bombard you: “Will we be laid off?” You don’t know the answer yourself yet.
The acquired company sends a list of “sacred traditions”: pizza Fridays, an office dog and a post-lunch nap.
The acquiring company’s CEO drops by your office “just to look around” and immediately asks for the seating plan. Is that a bad sign?
The lawyer reports the target company has an ongoing lawsuit its owners “forgot” to mention. Signing is today.
Morning. The merged company must pick one of two accounting systems. Each team considers theirs the pinnacle of creation.
At the first joint stand-up after the merger, the two companies’ managers sit strictly on opposite sides of the table. They even use different coffee machines.
In negotiations the target company’s owner wants “emotional value” included in the price. He values it at half the deal.
The auditors find a “ghost warehouse” in the target’s books: it exists on paper, but on site it’s a vacant lot full of daisies.
The merged company needs a name. Options: yours, theirs, or a new one from an AI. The AI suggests “Synergium.”
After the merger it turns out you now have two CFOs, two sales directors and two CMOs. Who stays?
At a meeting the buyer’s rep asks which of your employees are “irreplaceable.” He writes every name in his notebook.
The startup you’re buying demands its founder stay CEO of his division with veto power over everything. Even your lunch.
After the merger, staff from both companies argue over which party to keep: the New Year’s party or the summer picnic. Your call.
The antitrust authority requested deal documents and gave you three days. There are six thousand, and half are in a warehouse.
9 p.m. The merged company holds its first joint evening call. Half the participants turned off their cameras out of habit; the other half muted their mics.
In the evening the acquired company’s owner calls to complain that your people greet his people “wrong.” Too formal, he says.
right: Ask him to bear with it

text: Late at night you realize the merger left you with two Wi-Fi passwords, two anthems and two nearly identical logos. Unify?
The banker calls at 10:15 p.m.: the buyer “has some questions,” and they need answers by morning. There are sixty-two.
In the evening a team lead complains that the other team “doesn’t get our jokes.” He proposes a dedicated humor training.
The acquired company sent its final report. Their “key client” turns out to be the owner’s brother. The contract with him is verbal.
right: Admit the mistake to the board

text: At dinner you announce the family is “acquiring” the neighbor’s cat that keeps visiting. The announcement meets with little enthusiasm.
right: Leave the cat to the neighbors

text: Your inner voice warns that you’re buying a company in an industry you know nothing about. The board calls it “diversification.”
An employee of the acquired company writes you a personal email in the evening: he’s afraid of being “diluted.” He’s been there since day one.
In the evening the buyer cuts the price by 20%, citing “changing market conditions.” The market didn’t change today. Accept?
Evening. The merged company’s newsletter has an error: the signature shows your name with the title of the competitor you acquired.
The newly acquired team holds a “meet and greet” with yours. Their first question: “Is it true you’re going to lay us off?”
The merged sales team can’t decide who owns which clients. Three key clients now have two account managers each, and they all call at once.
The buyer’s lawyers review your documents and find a lease signed in 2009 with a glitter pen. Is it valid?
The new shared cafeteria. One company eats at noon, the other at 2 p.m. The cook makes everything twice and demands extra pay.
In the evening the founder of the acquired company calls: he misses his company and wants to buy it back. It’s been a week.
The board proposes buying a company that makes the same thing you do, only worse and pricier. The argument: “They have a nice sign.”
The merged company holds its first joint party. Your people are dancing; theirs are standing by the walls. Your people picked the music.
right: Let them get used to it

text: Late at night you discover the merged company has two websites with different prices for identical products. Customers noticed too.
The banker says the buyer wants to meet on “neutral ground.” Neutral ground is his country house.
The acquired company is rolling out its “code of conduct” at yours. Item twelve: a mandatory personal “good morning” to every employee.
In the evening both companies’ executives gather for an informal dinner. Your CFO and their CFO seem to be getting along. A little too well.
Your inner voice wonders: if the company merges, who will you be? No answer — just insomnia and cold tea.
Morning. A new employee from the merged company can’t find his desk. Under the new seating plan, his desk is your desk. Share it?
Late at night the auditor sends his report: the company you’re buying is worth half what was claimed. Signing is tomorrow.
At a trade show, the competitor you almost merged with is telling everyone he turned you down. Actually, you were the one who killed the deal.
Morning. The two accounting teams now share one room. Within an hour there’s a dispute over how documents should be fastened: paper clip or stapler.
In the evening the acquired company sends a photo of its party captioned “Celebrating freedom.” The deal closed this morning.
7:50 a.m. The CMO sends a photo: a competitor put up a billboard right across from your office. The slogan: “We’re never late.” Your move?
A competitor cut prices 30% across the board this morning. Sales is calling in a panic; clients are already asking about discounts. What now?
The analyst brings a report: a competitor launched the product you debated for six months and never approved. Even the name is similar.
The HR director reports a competitor is poaching your lead developer with double the pay. Today is his last day to “think it over.”
right: Let him go with best wishes

text: A competitor’s CEO calls at 8:00 and offers to agree on prices “as neighbors.” That’s illegal, and you both know it.
This morning’s industry newsletter headline: “Market Leader: Your Competitor.” The board has already forwarded it to you, no comment.
The sales director suggests “having a little fun” with online reviews of competitors. Anonymously, of course. It’s a bad idea.
right: Explain the risks to the team

text: You learn a competitor hired your former CFO. He knows all your numbers for the past five years.
At a morning conference you notice a competitor’s employee writing down your every word. You were just about to talk about plans.
Marketing brings a comparison table: “Us vs. the competitor.” We’re better at everything except price, quality and delivery times. Publish?
A competitor opened an office in your building, one floor up. This morning you’re in the elevator with their CEO. He’s smiling.
The analyst says a competitor spends three times more than you on advertising. The board asks why you’re being so modest.
At the trade show the competitor’s booth is twice as big as yours and has a live orchestra. Your booth is a table with flyers and a bowl of candy.
A competitor is suing you for “copying their packaging color.” Your packaging is green. So is theirs. So is half the market’s.
A key client tells the sales director a competitor offered him “a free trial year.” The client asks what you’ll offer.
At a conference a competitor publicly challenges you to a “friendly debate.” Topic: “Whose product is better.” The audience applauds. Accept?
Your new manager brings a competitor’s presentation he “accidentally” took from his last job. It has their strategy for the year.
A competitor proposes teaming up against a new market entrant. The alliance makes sense, but this competitor is known for betraying allies.
Marketing wants to run a “We’re not like them” campaign full of hints at the competitor. The lawyer is clutching his heart in advance.
A competitor opened a café right next to your office and hands your employees free coffee. With an HR business card attached.
The sales director proposes poaching the competitor’s top account manager. He’s willing, but wants the same salary as you.
9 p.m. The competitor’s CEO posts a photo from a meeting with your key client. Captioned “New horizons!”
In the evening a competitor reports 40% revenue growth. The board forwards the link: “And how are we doing?” We’re at 7%.
The HR director reports half the sales team interviewed with a competitor. They all came back — with offers in their pockets.
A competitor invites you to his company’s anniversary. On the program: he presents himself with a “Market Leadership” award.
Your inner voice suggests you stop stalking competitors every evening. You’ve spent three hours studying their job postings. Close the tab?
right: Write a report on their jobs

text: Your kid says the competitor CEO’s son is in his class. They’re friends and trade stickers.
At a restaurant in the evening, the competitor’s team is at the next table, loudly discussing their plans. You can hear every word.
Late at night a former employee who went to a competitor writes: “Can I come back?” He left in a scandal six months ago.
Evening message from the sales director: “The competitor promised our client a rocket, and we’ve only got a bicycle.” He wants a rocket by Monday.
In the evening a competitor emails you a message meant for his own board. It contains his strategy. Wrong recipient.
Industry awards night. You lost “Company of the Year” to a competitor. He gives thanks from the stage while looking right at you.
A competitor issued a press release comparing itself to you. It gets your prices, products and even your name wrong.
Your former deputy, now a director at a competitor, invites you to lunch, “just to talk about old times.” He orders on your tab.
In the evening you learn the competitor has a new CEO: your old classmate who copied off you during exams. Call to congratulate him?
First thing in the morning the sales director wants to hire a “scout” to attend competitor events posing as a client.
right: Send him to a public webinar

text: Your inner voice suggests your main competitor is yesterday’s you. Sounds lovely, but the board wants numbers, not quotes.
In the evening a competitor emails your clients: “We miss you.” Half of them have never worked with him.
The industry association proposes that you and a competitor co-chair the standards committee. Meetings are on Saturdays.
At a meeting a major client compares you out loud to a competitor and calls you “like them, but pricier.” His deputy nods.
8:00 a.m. The board chair calls to discuss your “leadership style.” He heard you’re too soft a leader. He won’t say from whom.
The owner says he’s decided to sell the company, but doesn’t know to whom. He wants it “ready for sale” within a month. Secretly.
right: Persuade him to tell the team

text: Morning leadership meeting. Each of the nine directors reports for ten minutes, and each one starts with “Quickly.”
Your assistant brings today’s schedule: eighteen meetings and one line that says “lunch,” squeezed between two board sessions. Optimize?
Your first deputy announces he wants to be CEO. Not here, just in general. But here would work too. How do you react?
The press office wants a video address to staff about the quarter’s results. The results are bad, but the address must “inspire.”
The board wants a weekly one-page “company pulse.” The company’s pulse is jittery, but the page must look calm.
The CFO shows you the cash flow chart. It looks like a cardiogram. The board hates charts like that. Redraw it?
Security won’t let you into the office: your badge was blocked after the access system was replaced. A line of employees is forming behind you.
The external auditors ask you to “just confirm” a hundred and forty figures in the annual report. Each with your signature. By lunch.
You’re late to your own morning meeting: stuck in the elevator with a board member. He uses the time to discuss your bonus.
The corporate lawyer asks you to sign a power of attorney in his name, “just in case.” It gives him the right to sell the building.
The board decides you need an “executive coach.” At the first session the coach asks you to draw your inner world. Do you?
At the meeting directors argue over whose turn it is to take the blame for the quarter. Each points at his neighbor. The neighbor points at the weather.
The owner wants by tonight a list of three employees to promote and three to let go. No explanations, “by gut feeling.”
The lawyer reports an employee has sued for unpaid overtime. The documents confirm it: he worked late nights on your instructions.
Midday, the website that brings in 70% of sales goes down. The CTO is on a plane and his deputy is on vacation. Your move?
A business newspaper reporter wants an interview about “the company’s difficulties.” There are difficulties, but the interview could double them. Agree?
The owner decided every decision over $100,000 must be approved by him personally. His phone is available Tuesdays from 11 to 12.
The board wants you to personally address the all-staff meeting and explain why there will be no bonuses. The mic is ready.
In the evening you’re told that the next board meeting will discuss a “CEO performance review.” Without you present.
At home you learn the August vacation clashes with a board meeting. The tickets are bought and nonrefundable.
The owner writes at 10 p.m.: “Why aren’t you at the office? I’m at the office.” He stopped by for forgotten keys and decided to check who’s working.
Your inner voice asks if you remember why you became a leader. All you remember is that you once wanted to “make an impact.” Make an impact on your sleep?
Your deputy leaves at 6 p.m. every day and doesn’t answer messages after that. The board thinks you spoil him.
The evening directors’ meeting drags on: the CFO and the sales director are competing over who’s louder. It’s been ninety minutes.
In the evening you’re invited to speak at a leadership forum. Topic: “Finding Work-Life Balance.” You have no balance.
In the evening the lawyer writes that an order you signed contradicts another order — also yours — from last month. Which one goes?
For your birthday, staff gave you a mug reading “Best CEO.” In fine print beneath: “according to those who want a bonus.”
In the evening the board chair advises you to “rest more.” Five minutes later he sends four tasks for the weekend.
The owner asks you to accompany him to an evening charity auction and “help him choose.” He’s already eyeing a painting worth your annual bonus.
At 11 p.m. you realize you forgot to congratulate the CFO on the company anniversary. He congratulated everyone but you. Oops.
In the evening your assistant says she’s going on maternity leave in a week — and only she knows where the key contracts are and how your calendar works.
left: Write it all down this week

text: The press office wants approval for a social post: a photo of you “at work.” In it you’re eating a sandwich over your keyboard.
Your inner voice suggests turning off your phone this weekend. The board, the owner and the investors suggest otherwise. Who wins?
After a hard day you find a note from the cleaner in your office: “Don’t worry, it’ll all work out.” She knows more about the company than the board.
8:10 a.m. A fund that turned you down a year ago writes: “We’ve been following you and would like to reopen the conversation.” Your valuation has doubled.
In the morning you learn the video conferencing subscription was canceled to save money. The board joins in fifteen minutes.
A key client says his new procurement manager is “reviewing all suppliers.” The procurement manager is twenty-three and very serious.
The morning after the merger. Staff from the two companies use different messengers and can’t see each other’s messages. The meeting falls apart.
A shareholder sends a question: “Why did you buy a new printer?” The printer costs less than his ticket to the shareholders’ meeting.
You learn a competitor patented an idea your R&D department shelved “for better times.” Better times arrived — for the competitor.
Morning. You discover the company website still shows a ten-year-old mission: “To become the leader in the pager market.”
The CFO reports that the Q3 budget was used up in Q1. The reason: “unforeseen foreseeable expenses.”
An investor asks you to speak at his conference about “the secrets of success.” So far, the slide with your secrets just says “luck.”
The board approved an acquisition on condition that your deputy runs it. You’ll “oversee.” Is that a promotion or a demotion?
The board wants to cut rent and proposes moving half the office to remote work. Staff are for it, but the owner likes seeing people.
A foreign partner offers a big contract, but negotiates only through an interpreter who clearly abridges everything.
Your salesperson brings news: a competitor launched a product with your exact name, but a different last letter. Customers are confused.
At the budget committee the CIO finally admits “cloud migration — ∞” meant “I have no idea how much.” The committee falls silent.
left: Give him a month to cost it
right: Cut the line to the minimum

text: The merged dev team is arguing about whether curly braces go on the same line or the next. The dispute has reached you.
left: Settle it with a coin toss

text: In the evening an investor congratulates you on a good quarter and immediately asks why it wasn’t twice as good. Reply?
A poll appears in the shareholders’ group: “Do you trust the CEO?” Voting is public. Watch the results?
The owner sends a voice message from a restaurant: “Let’s buy this restaurant.” He liked it. The company makes pipes.
right: Gently talk him out of it

text: In the evening the company shuttle driver says the last run was canceled to save money. Twenty employees are still in the office after 9 p.m.
Late at night a client emails: “We’re ready, but our board wants to review everything once more.” His board meets once a quarter.
At home your kid is playing “CEO” and holding a meeting with his toys. He tells them in your voice: “This is not up for discussion.” Time to reflect?
In the evening a board member calls to ask advice about his own private business. It’s a two-hour question unrelated to your company.
In the evening a recruiter offers you the CEO job at a competitor, 40% more pay. Respond?
Your inner voice sums up the week: three board meetings, two investors, one merger and zero hours of sleep. Time to change something?
In the evening the CFO sends a vacation photo: he made it to the beach after all. In the photo: a laptop on a sun lounger and the quarterly report.
right: Ask him to send the report

text: Late at night you realize you didn’t complete a single task from your list today, but attended eleven meetings.
In the evening the press office asks you to comment on a rumor that the company is being sold. The rumor is true, but the deal hasn’t been announced.
In the evening your deputy admits that a week ago he missed an important email from an investor. The reply was due yesterday.
